passages.happening:
On the third day there is a wedding at Cana in Galilee. Jesus' mother is there, and Jesus and his disciples have been invited too. Then the wine runs out. His mother tells him, “They have no more wine” (verse 3).

Jesus answers, “Woman, why does this concern us?” and adds, “My hour has not yet come” (verse 4). His mother turns to the servants and says, “Do whatever He tells you” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
A village wedding was the biggest celebration most families ever held, and it could go on for days; Samson's wedding feast lasted seven (Judges 14:12). The groom's family was expected to provide. To run out of wine was more than awkward. In a world that cared greatly about honour and shame, it would be remembered against the family for years.

Wine was the normal drink of a feast, and a sign of God's goodness. A psalm praises God for “wine that gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15). It was usually mixed with water. Scripture warns plainly against drunkenness (Proverbs 20:1; Ephesians 5:18), but it never calls wine itself evil.

‘Woman’ sounds cold in English. It was not. It was a polite way to speak to a woman, something like ‘madam’. Jesus uses it for the Samaritan woman (4:21) and for Mary Magdalene at the tomb (20:15). He will use it to his mother again from the cross, as he gives her into his friend's care (19:26).

The words that follow are a Hebrew way of saying ‘this is not ours to deal with’. The Old Testament has the same phrase; the Berean Standard Bible gives it as “What have I to do with you” in 2 Samuel 16:10. It sets a request aside, but not always coldly. And Mary does not hear a refusal. She tells the servants to do what he says.
passages.ot: The Old Testament often pictures God and his people as a bride and groom: “as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5). A wedding where the wine has run out makes a sad picture of a people waiting for joy that has not yet come. In the next chapter John the Baptist will call Jesus the bridegroom (3:29).
passages.hard: Did Jesus refuse, and then change his mind? Some readers think so. Others think he would not act on his family's timing or for his family's sake, and then acted in his own way, so quietly that only the servants knew. Christians weigh Mary's part differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often see her here as one who brings other people's needs to her Son. Many Protestants stress the distance Jesus keeps between his hour and his family's request. All can agree on her words, which may be the best advice in the book: ‘Do whatever He tells you’.
passages.asks: Mary does not tell Jesus what to do. She tells him what is wrong, and then tells others to obey him. That is a good way to pray: name the need, and leave the how and the when to him. Is there a need you have been trying to fix on your own that you could bring to him instead?

passages.t: Water into wine, the first sign
passages.happening:
Six stone water jars stand nearby, set there for ‘the Jewish rites of purification’. Each holds twenty to thirty gallons (verse 6). Jesus tells the servants, “Fill the jars with water,” and they fill them to the brim. Then he tells them to draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet.

The master tastes it, and it is wine. He does not know where it came from, though the servants do. He calls the groom over. Everyone serves the fine wine first, he says, and the cheap wine later. ‘But you have saved the fine wine until now’ (verse 10).

John adds a closing line. This was the first of Jesus' signs. He did it at Cana in Galilee. He revealed his glory, and his disciples believed in him (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Stone jars like these have been found in many places in Jewish Galilee and Judea. Under the law, a clay pot that became unclean had to be broken (Leviticus 11:33). But many Jews believed that stone could not become unclean, and a rule later written down in the Mishnah, around AD 200, says the same (Kelim 10:1). So stone jars kept water ready for washing hands and dishes, to keep God's law of purity.

Do the sums. Six jars of twenty to thirty gallons make 120 to 180 gallons of wine, near the end of a feast. That is far more than anyone needed. It is a picture of overflowing gift.

The master of the banquet was the guest in charge of the tables and the wine. His joke in verse 10 is about what hosts usually do; it does not say that these guests were drunk. And notice who knows the secret. Not the master, not the groom, but the servants who did the work.
passages.ot: The prophets pictured the day of God's coming as a time of overflowing wine. “The mountains will drip with sweet wine” (Amos 9:13; also Joel 3:18), and God will prepare for all peoples “a feast of aged wine” (Isaiah 25:6). Many readers think John wants us to hear those promises at Cana: the best wine has been kept until now. Some also notice that water kept for washing has become wine for a wedding. What the old washings were waiting for has come.
passages.hard:
Is this story for drinking or against it? Neither, really. Some Christians who do not drink have argued that the wine was unfermented grape juice. Most scholars think the Greek word for wine (oinos) and the master's remark mean real wine. On the other side, the story gives no approval to drunkenness, which Scripture condemns. The story is not about drinking. It is about Jesus bringing the joy God had promised.

If alcohol has hurt you or your family, this story is not asking you to drink, and the joy it shows is in Jesus, not in a cup. If drinking has become hard to control, you do not have to face it alone. Tell someone you trust, and reach out to a doctor or a recovery group near you.
passages.asks: Jesus' first sign saved a family from shame, quietly, through servants who did what he said. Before it was a miracle, it was ordinary obedience: filling jars with water. What ordinary thing has he asked of you that you have not done, because it seemed too small to matter?

passages.happening:
After a few days in Capernaum with his mother, his brothers and his disciples, Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for the Passover. In the temple courts he finds men selling cattle, sheep and doves, and money changers sitting at their tables.

He makes a whip out of cords and drives them all out, with the sheep and the cattle. He pours out the coins and turns over the tables. To the dove sellers he says, “Get these out of here! How dare you turn My Father's house into a marketplace!” (verse 16). His disciples remember the words of a psalm: “Zeal for Your house will consume Me” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The trade was legal and useful. Pilgrims came from far away and needed animals for sacrifice. Doves were the offering the poor could afford (Leviticus 12:8). Every Jewish man paid a yearly half shekel to the temple (Exodus 30:13), and it was paid in the silver shekels of Tyre, so other coins had to be changed. The selling most likely went on in the great outer court, the one part of the temple that non-Jews, called Gentiles, could enter.

So why such anger? Jesus calls the temple ‘My Father's house’. He acts not as a reformer from outside, but as a son in his own father's home. And the place for meeting God had become a market.

The whip of cords was made on the spot. John says Jesus drove out the sheep and the cattle with it. He does not say Jesus struck anyone. This was a sign done in public, like the acted signs of the prophets of old.
passages.ot: Psalm 69 is the prayer of a man who suffers because he loves God's house: “zeal for Your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me” (Psalm 69:9). The psalm says ‘has consumed’; John's Greek says ‘will consume’. Many readers think the change points ahead. Jesus' love for his Father's house will cost him his life. The prophet Malachi had also said, “Then the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple” (Malachi 3:1).
passages.hard: John tells of Jesus clearing the temple near the start of his work, while Matthew, Mark and Luke put it in the last week (Mark 11:15-19). Some think it happened twice: John has Jesus in Jerusalem at several feasts, and the words he speaks are different, ‘a marketplace’ here and ‘a den of robbers’ in the others. Others think John placed one event early for reasons of his own, as a headline for the whole story. These notes do not settle it. Either way, the meaning is the same in all four Gospels: Jesus has authority over God's house.
passages.asks: Jesus was angry because a house of prayer had become a place of trade. Anger at wrong can be right, but this scene is not permission for our tempers. It is a son's zeal for his Father's honour. Where has your own worship turned into a kind of trade, doing things for God in order to get something back?

passages.happening:
Some of the leaders demand, “What sign can You show us to prove Your authority to do these things?” (verse 18). Jesus answers, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again” (verse 19).

They think he means the building. “This temple took forty-six years to build,” they say, and you will raise it in three days? (verse 20). But John explains: Jesus was speaking about the temple of his body (verse 21). After he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this. Then they believed the Scripture and the word Jesus had spoken (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
‘The Jews’ in verses 18 and 20 are the temple leaders. Their question was a fair one: anyone acting like a prophet in the temple might be asked for a sign.

‘Forty-six years’ fits what we know. The Jewish historian Josephus says that Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple in the eighteenth year of his reign, about 20 or 19 BC (Antiquities 15.380). Forty-six years from then is about AD 27 or 28. Work on the outer buildings went on long after that.

John uses a different Greek word for ‘temple’ here than in verses 14 and 15. There it meant the whole temple area, with its courts. Here it means the inner house of God itself, the sanctuary. Jesus says his body is that house: the place where God lives among his people.

John says openly that the disciples did not understand at the time. They understood after Easter, by remembering (he says the same in 12:16). Jesus later promised that the Spirit would “remind you of everything I have told you” (14:26).
passages.ot: In the Old Testament the temple was the place of God's presence: when Solomon's temple was dedicated, “the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 8:11). John says that God's presence now lives in Jesus himself. Jesus' words were later remembered, and twisted. At his trial witnesses claimed he had said, ‘I will destroy this man-made temple’ (Mark 14:58), and people at the cross mocked him with it (Mark 15:29). But Jesus had not said ‘I will destroy’. He said ‘Destroy this temple’, and promised to raise it. John does not say which Scripture the disciples came to believe (verse 22). Later the apostles read Psalm 16:10, “nor will You let Your Holy One see decay”, as a promise of the resurrection (Acts 2:27-31).
passages.hard: Did Jesus raise himself? Here he says, ‘I will raise it up’. Elsewhere the New Testament says, “God raised Him from the dead” (Acts 2:24). John holds both. Jesus says he has authority to lay down his life and to take it up again, and that this charge came from his Father (10:18). The Father and the Son act together.
passages.asks: The disciples understood Jesus' words only later, looking back. Faith often works that way. Some things God says make sense only after the cross and the empty tomb, and some only years later in your own life. What word of his are you holding now that you do not yet understand?

passages.t: He knew what was in a man
passages.happening: While Jesus is in Jerusalem for the Passover feast, many people see the signs he is doing and believe in his name. But Jesus does not entrust himself to them, because he knows them all. He does not need anyone to tell him about people, for he knows what is in a man (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
John plays on one word here. ‘Believe’ and ‘entrust’ are the same Greek verb. Many ‘believed’ in him, but he did not ‘believe himself’ to them. Their trust was real but thin, built on the wonders they had seen.

The very next verse (3:1) begins, “Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus”. John has just said that Jesus knew what was in a man. Now he shows us one.
passages.ot: Only God knows the heart. When Samuel looked at David's tall brother, God told him, “man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). Jeremiah says, “The heart is deceitful above all things”, and then God says, “I, the LORD, search the heart” (Jeremiah 17:9-10). John says that Jesus knows what is in a man. He does not need to be told.
passages.hard: Is faith that starts with miracles false? No. The disciples' own faith started with a sign (verse 11). What Jesus does not trust is excitement that goes no deeper. Faith that starts with wonders has to grow into trust in Jesus himself.
passages.asks: Jesus knows what is in you: the real faith and the half faith, the hope and the fear. That could be frightening. But in the next chapter he spends a whole night with a man whose faith is only half formed. Being fully known by him is where being helped begins.
